# Population ecology — growth, regulation, interactions

## 1. Introduction
Opening frame for **Population ecology — growth** — what the topic is, why it matters, a real-world hook (Nepal where possible), the map of what follows, and the learning outcomes (biology-plan.md §3.1, block I). Prose depth is written in the Organisms and Environment fill pass.

## 2. Hierarchy body — every syllabus sub-point
### Population ecology — growth
### regulation
### interactions

Fill order per concept: definition → structure → process → significance (§3.2). Step-by-step numbered points, Pioneer style.

A **population** is a group of individuals of one species in one place and time. Its size (N) changes by four processes: natality (+), mortality (−), immigration (+), emigration (−). Growth follows two models — unlimited **exponential** growth or **logistic** growth limited by carrying capacity (K). Populations also interact: competition, predation, parasitism, commensalism, mutualism and amensalism.

## 3. Classified tables

Tables carry examples in every classification and characteristics row, ≤ 12 rows, and each is referenced from the body text (§3.3).

**Concept flow — from population size to interaction types (study in this order)**

| Step | Concept | Key equation / example |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Population attributes | N = size; density; birth rate, death rate; sex ratio; age pyramids |
| 2 | Four processes change N | Natality + immigration − mortality − emigration |
| 3 | Exponential growth (unlimited resources) | dN/dt = rN; J-shaped curve |
| 4 | Logistic growth (real world) | dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K; S-shaped curve |
| 5 | Carrying capacity K | Maximum sustainable population for the habitat |
| 6 | Regulation | Density-dependent factors (disease, competition) pull N back toward K |
| 7 | Interspecific interactions | Six pairs — see the classified table below |

**Population interactions — who wins and who loses**

| Interaction | Species A | Species B | Example |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mutualism | + | + | Mycorrhiza and plant; lichen alga + fungus; fig and wasp |
| Commensalism | + | 0 | Cattle egret and cattle; barnacles on whale |
| Predation | + | − | Tiger and deer; also herbivores on plants |
| Parasitism | + | − | Flea on dog; Plasmodium in human; cuckoo brood parasitism |
| Competition | − | − | Gause's Paramecium experiment; invasive species ousting natives |
| Amensalism | 0 | − | Penicillium inhibits bacteria; shading by a large tree |

**Exponential vs logistic growth; r- vs K-strategists**

| Feature | Exponential (J-curve) | Logistic (S-curve) |
|---|---|---|
| Resources | Unlimited (never true for long) | Limited — the real world |
| Equation | dN/dt = rN | dN/dt = rN(K − N)/K |
| Final outcome | Explosion, then crash | Stabilises at carrying capacity K |
| Example | Bacteria in fresh broth; reindeer introduced to island |

## 5. Worked examples and applications
≥ 6 worked examples with solved steps, live examples and Nepal-context applications (biology-plan.md §3.1, block V) — written in the unit fill pass.

## 6. Key terms and statements
Every new term defined once; exam-grade definitions live here and in keyPoints (block VI).

**Worked example — Gause's competition.** Two *Paramecium* species grown together in one tube: *P. aurelia* outgrows *P. caudatum*, which dies out — **competitive exclusion**: two species with the same niche cannot coexist. In nature the loser survives by **resource partitioning** (different microhabitat, different feeding time). This one experiment explains why invasive species are so destructive: they occupy the native species' niche without its predators.

## 7. Exam Zone
NEB past-question map (long/short), topic-wise MCQs with explanations, and short tricks (block VII). Existing entrance-exam (CEE) material stays where it is; this zone grows around it — see the seeded exam fields of this file when present.

**Most-asked points (NEB).** (1) Define population and list the four processes that change its size. (2) Write both growth equations and draw both curves. (3) Define carrying capacity. (4) Tabulate the six interactions with signs (+/−/0) and one example each. (5) Explain competitive exclusion and resource partitioning. (6) Contrast r- and K-strategists.

examShortTricks: Trick 1: Growth equations: exponential dN/dt = rN (J-curve, unlimited); logistic dN/dt = rN(K−N)/K (S-curve, carrying capacity K) — quote both equations and their curve shapes.
Trick 2: r-strategists: small, short-lived, many offspring, unstable habitat; K-strategists: large, few offspring, stable habitat — the contrast pair.
Trick 3: Interactions table: mutualism (+/+), competition (−/−), predation (+/−), parasitism (+/−), commensalism (+/0), amensalism (−/0) — six signs, six marks.
Trick 4: Gause's principle: two species with identical niches cannot coexist — competitive exclusion; resource partitioning is the escape.
